fields.question: Why score true RoPE pairs with Q/K norm products rather than K magnitude alone?
fields.answer: Attention error depends on both query and key. Score each rotation plane jointly to preserve coupling. Choose high-precision pairs per shared KV head during prefill and reuse them without future decode data. Memory adjacency need not be a true pair.
fields.example: A large key direction rarely used by queries may not deserve precision; adjacent Llama channels need not rotate together.

fields.question: Why assign higher precision to some RoPE pairs?
fields.answer: Rotation planes differ in QK impact. Prefill average Q/K norm products estimate importance, and each KV head fixes its high-precision set, trading cache width for attention error.
fields.example: Preserve both dimensions of a high-impact rotation pair together.

fields.question: Are PN-Mix 1-bit correction and FP16 residual buffering the same?
fields.answer: No. Correction shifts 1-bit reconstruction bins without extra residual codes. The buffer holds new not-yet-quantized tokens. They have distinct numerical and storage roles.
fields.example: Corrected quantized groups can coexist with a new full-precision token batch.

fields.question: Can Llama/SmolLM2 RoPE pairs be formed from adjacent coordinates?
fields.answer: No for split-half layout: pair corresponding coordinates across the halves, unlike interleaved layout. Pin the prefill-selected mask across pages, without decode lookahead.
fields.example: Pair index i in the first half with index i in the second, not necessarily i+1.

fields.question: Why add a recoverable quantized tier between full precision and deletion?
fields.answer: Attention relevance can drift. Lower storage preserves approximate content for promotion when accumulated attention rises. Permanent deletion cannot recover it; dequantization does not restore lost precision. Local state checks are not serving performance.
fields.example: Demote an old clue, then read it again when a later question needs it.

fields.question: Why have full, recoverable quantized, and deleted states?
fields.answer: The middle tier keeps dormant history available with less storage and supports promotion under renewed attention, unlike deletion.
fields.example: A previously irrelevant window can return to high-priority reading.

fields.question: Is promotion from quantized cache equivalent to never quantizing it?
fields.answer: Not necessarily. Dequantization restores access, not every original bit. Measure quantization error separately from the advantage over deletion.
fields.example: Converting a low-bit vector to float does not restore original decimals.

fields.question: What should QEvict verify when cumulative scores update?
fields.answer: Verify decay γ, current attention increments, promotion threshold, and slot budget. Keep actual recoverable quantized content. A log state alone does not migrate data.
fields.example: Crossing τ should restore the stored vector, not just increment a count.

fields.question: Why keep original RoPE frequencies and head scaling after RACE narrows attention?
fields.answer: This is a subspace of an existing model. Preserve complete matched Q/K rotation pairs, original frequencies and width scaling; fold V projections into weights for native low-dimensional compute. Calibration energy optimizes a bound, not global LM loss.
fields.example: Keep original second and fifth frequencies rather than renumbering them first and second.

fields.question: Why directly reduce native attention head width?
fields.answer: Low-rank storage followed by full reconstruction saves memory but adds work. RACE folds selections and V subspaces into projections so attention runs on retained dimensions.
fields.example: Run four-dimensional attention directly instead of rebuilding eight dimensions.

fields.question: Why compress Q/K in pairs but V with an SVD subspace?
fields.answer: Q/K preserve common RoPE planes and matching geometry. Values carry aggregated content and can use a calibrated right singular space. One common pruning rule changes their roles.
fields.example: Keep the corresponding K pair for each Q pair; V need not use those coordinates.

fields.question: Why fold W_O when compressing V?
fields.answer: W_V′=W_VP_V and W_O′=P_VᵀW_O define one subspace path. Changing V alone mismatches shape or function. Detach calibration and SVD while retaining gradients through folded forward.
fields.example: A four-dimensional V needs a matching output map, not the original eight-dimensional interpretation.

fields.question: Why protect full prompts but sample generated history independently per head?
fields.answer: Prompt preservation keeps task conditions and initial evidence fixed. Per-head random retention avoids scoring and gives diverse coverage, but may miss important reasoning and must fit the protected prompt budget. GPU reconstruction is not full task or kernel evaluation.
fields.example: Different heads can see different reasoning fragments while all still read the original question.

fields.question: Why omit KV importance scoring in Random Attention?
fields.answer: Scoring costs compute and can impose one shared ranking. Protect the prompt and sample generated positions uniformly per head as a simpler cache trade-off.
fields.example: Keep part of each head's history without scanning all tokens for importance first.

fields.question: How does independent per-head sampling differ from a shared random set?
fields.answer: Head-specific sets vary evidence coverage; shared sampling applies one restriction everywhere. Average budgets can match while errors and coverage correlations differ.
fields.example: One head can keep position five and another eight.

fields.question: May the method drop prompt entries if B is smaller than prompt length?
fields.answer: Not under full prompt protection. B−|P| must be a valid generation budget. Raise the budget or report infeasibility rather than changing the method silently.
fields.example: A 100-entry prompt cannot fit untouched into 80 slots.

fields.question: Why can a remote KV hit be slower than re-prefill?
fields.answer: Fetch has fixed request latency and volume-dependent transfer; recompute depends on prefill throughput. Break-even depends on length and bandwidth, and asynchronous shards must avoid head-of-line blocking. Hit rate is not latency. No local remote implementation or GPU results.
fields.example: A short hit can spend more time opening the connection than local recompute takes.

fields.question: Why analyze fetch versus re-prefill break-even first?
fields.answer: Remote hits pay request and transfer costs; GPU recompute can be fast. Compare both paths by length and bandwidth, not only hit rate.
fields.example: Fetching a short cached prefix can be slower than recreating KV.

fields.question: Does B>sR with fixed T0 guarantee fetch is faster at every length?
fields.answer: No. It gives asymptotic bandwidth advantage. Compare T0+sn/B against n/R for finite requests; fixed cost can dominate short ones.
fields.example: Fast per-token transfer does not erase first-packet latency.

fields.question: Why use per-PCP-rank remote instances and async loading?
fields.answer: MLA cache is sharded by rank; independent instances and async loads reduce head-of-line blocking. Validation needs the multi-node service and workload, not a single A100/A30 fixture.
fields.example: A large request on one rank should not hold a small load on another.

fields.question: Why commit only accepted inputs and keep a high-precision anchor separate from low-precision reads?
fields.answer: Replay outputs from a checkpoint and short input log without full writes every token. Rejected drafts cannot enter committed state. Refresh from the high-precision anchor and raw records to avoid rounding feedback. Reassociation preserves recurrence dependencies.
fields.example: Accept two of four drafts and advance only two steps; do not refresh from the rejected tail or rounded copy.

fields.question: Why cache small inputs instead of writing a full matrix each token?
fields.answer: Matrix-state traffic can be bandwidth-bound. Refresh periodically and record inputs for reassociated reads, especially output-only speculative checks.
fields.example: Store one anchor and several small inputs instead of a whole matrix per step.

fields.question: How should output-only replay match stepwise recurrence?
fields.answer: Compute equivalent readout without materializing each state. Persistent refresh uses only committed inputs. Computation and writes change, not the reference accepted sequence.
fields.example: Match ordinary recurrence on accepted tokens; rejected drafts affect neither committed state.

fields.question: Why preserve raw values and recompute residuals when refreshing GDN?
fields.answer: Residuals depend on the precise anchor. Reusing rounded reads or stale residuals feeds error back. Refresh from committed raw records and separately produce high/low copies; zero accepted tokens leave the anchor unchanged.
fields.example: Rejected drafts may have computed outputs without updating committed recurrence.

fields.question: Why distill on the quantized student's prefixes with per-candidate KL mixing?
fields.answer: Quantization changes visited states, so score the student's own prefixes. Teacher/student probability ratios mix forward and reverse KL per candidate to treat over- and underestimation differently. Detach mixture weights and retain a residual mass bucket.
fields.example: A correct number underweighted and a connective overweighted at one position need different coefficients, not ideal teacher prefixes.
